articles.title_orig: Strong demand in China boosts US exporters
articles.title_zh: Strong demand in China boosts US exporters
articles.content_orig:
Appetite for high-quality goods fueling opportunities amid reciprocal tariff cuts
China's growing appetite for high-quality consumer goods and industrial inputs is drawing more products from the United States into its market, as holiday spending, industrial upgrading and the recent reciprocal tariff-cut arrangement offer US exporters more room to expand sales in the country, according to trade experts and business leaders.
From fresh fruit and seafood to integrated circuits and energy products, US shipments to China have remained substantial, reflecting the complementary nature of the two economies and the potential for expanding imports to support more balanced and mutually beneficial bilateral trade, they said.
The trend was particularly visible during the National Day holiday from Oct 1 to Wednesday, as stronger demand for food and other consumer products prompted Chinese importers to step up purchases from overseas suppliers.
READ MORE: Sino-US trade gets reciprocal tariff cut boost
Oheng Supply Chain Management (Ningbo) Co, a cross-border food products importer based in Ningbo, Zhejiang province, imported 44.62 million yuan ($6.66 million) worth of products, including fresh cherries and fish oil from the US, in the first eight months of 2026.
Ahead of the holiday, shipments of US fish oil, red yeast rice, fresh cherries and grapes purchased by the company arrived in China to replenish supplies for the holiday market.
"The US is one of our main sources for products such as fish oil and cherries, with stable supply capacity," said Zhou Shouming, the company's director of customs affairs. "Judging from our sales, domestic consumers' demand for high-quality imported food continues to grow."
In late September, China and the US released reciprocal tariff-cut lists covering about $30 billion worth of imports from each side. Zhou said that the arrangement will lower costs for products including fresh cherries and grapes and give the company greater flexibility in pricing, allowing it to bring more high-quality US food products to Chinese buyers.
Pistachios are also included on China's tariff-cut list. Nut growers in California are expected to export 111,000 metric tons of pistachios to China in the 2026 crop year (Sept 1,2026 to Aug 31, 2027), according to Wonderful Pistachios & Almonds, the largest pistachio producer by production volume and sales revenue in the US.
Anita Lam, managing director for China at Wonderful Pistachios, said the industry remains confident about the long-term growth potential for California pistachios in the Chinese market, adding that her company will continue to leverage its vertically integrated supply chain and long-standing operations to deepen its presence in the country.
China's demand has also been strong for fresh seafood. Imports of US lobsters through Ningbo Lishe International Airport were valued at 200 million yuan between January and August, surging 468.5 percent year-on-year, according to Ningbo Customs.
Li Yongguo, president of Hengsheng Supply Chain (Dongguan) Co, a Dongguan, Guangdong province-based trading company, said that beyond food products, China's demand for imported integrated circuits has continued to grow, fueled by the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure and rising demand from the country's electronics manufacturing sector.
The Chinese company imported 10.31 billion yuan worth of integrated circuits from the US in the first three quarters, up 74.2 percent year-on-year, statistics from Huangpu Customs in Guangdong showed.
Miao Yingchun, a researcher at Wuhan University's Institute for International Studies in Wuhan, Hubei province, said China's demand for US products is being driven by both consumption and production — consumers seeking a wider range of quality goods and manufacturers requiring raw materials, components and equipment.
Wang Huiyao, president of the Beijing-based think tank Center for China and Globalization, noted that the Chinese and US economies are deeply interconnected.
"If the two countries can expand tariff reductions in specific areas and establish effective trade and investment mechanisms, even relatively limited steps at the outset could help strengthen confidence and pave the way for broader cooperation," he said.
China-US trade rose 5.5 percent year-on-year to $400.84 billion during the January-to-August period, while China's imports from the US grew 3.4 percent year-on-year, data from the General Administration of Customs showed.
The resilience of bilateral trade is also reflected in recent research. China's expanding import market continues to offer opportunities for US companies despite shifts in global trade and persistent bilateral economic tensions, according to a new report released in Los Angeles.
The report, "The Evolution of the Structure of US Exports to China and the Extended Effects Index from a CIIE Perspective (2026)", was released earlier this week at the Bridge to Shanghai: Business Opportunities with China event, part of an overseas outreach series ahead of the ninth China International Import Expo, which will be held from Nov 5 to 10.
ALSO READ: Imports poised to hit record high
The report says that the composition of trade also points to continuing economic complementarity between the world's two largest economies. It identifies China as the largest overseas market for US soybeans and cotton this year, and an important market for US integrated circuits and medical devices.
It also says the US remains a major source of China's services imports and has maintained a surplus in bilateral services trade.
Those patterns, according to the researchers, underscore the enduring commercial ties between the two economies even as tariffs, technology restrictions and changes in global sourcing have altered the bilateral trade landscape.
Li Qingjuan, director of the Think Tank Center at Fudan University's Fudan International School of Finance, said the CIIE is no longer simply about bringing products into the Chinese market. Instead, it has evolved into a global platform for companies to showcase their products, connect with potential partners and explore business opportunities.

articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.content_orig:

Mandatory evacuations have been announced and schools closed across parts of coastal Florida after Isaias intensified into the Atlantic season's first hurricane , advancing towards the US Gulf Coast Thursday, the National Hurricane Center said.
Forecasters warned that Isaias could deliver destructive hurricane-force winds to the Florida Panhandle, alongside southern Alabama and southern Mississippi.
“A life-threatening storm surge is expected from the Mouth of the Mississippi River to Suwannee, Florida. Residents in the warning area should follow advice given by local officials and evacuate immediately if told to do so,” the National Weather Service said Thursday.
“Damaging wind gusts are possible over much of central and northern Alabama and portions of western and northern Georgia, especially in areas of higher terrain,’ the NWS continued.
It could also cause a life-threatening storm surge along areas of the northern Gulf Coast, while potentially bringing heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) across the central Gulf Coast, according to the hurricane center.
An advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center said the cyclone’s center was positioned approximately 740 kilometres (460 miles) south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River , carrying maximum sustained winds of around 121 kph (75 mph).
After the storm initially formed earlier Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening.
Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.
The National Weather Service told communities from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Gulf County, Florida, to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages.”
Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, nearly tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.
Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday about 25 per cent of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
In Alabama, the cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.
Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground. Her family planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”

articles.title_orig: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
articles.title_zh: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
articles.content_orig:
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly.
Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.
Fort Hood attacker to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The shooting on 5 November 2009 took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
At court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution.
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened.
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.
Eugene R Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School, told the BBC it was a "really unfortunate decision".
"To livestream an execution is just so out of the Middle Ages. In a way, we are so past that as a society, at least I thought so until today," he said.
Fidell said if Hasan pursued legal action, the "proceedings would last years" and "far longer than President Trump's term in the White House".
Public execution is 'out of the Middle Ages', says Yale professor
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says.
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-restricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing.
It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content.
Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X, the most notable and widely used online platforms capable of streaming live video, have prohibitions in place on not only violent images and videos, but those that show death.
Meta, the owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment.
TikTok has a similar blanket ban. Its policy reads, "We don't allow extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing contentâespecially when it could cause viewers emotional distress."
The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since Elon Musk took over the platform, says that any content depicting when a person dies will be removed "if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative."
The BBC has reached out for comment to the companies.
Truth Social, the social media platform owned by Trump, does not have a live-stream video feature for users.
The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.
While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the group dubbed the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated.
Trump has previously condemned public executions in Iran, and has cited the Iranian government's potential killing of protesters as a possible justification for military intervention before attacking the country earlier this year.
The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions.
Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety".
The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the World War Two.

articles.title_orig: Former Greentown China head charged for bribes over stake in real estate project
articles.title_zh: Former Greentown China head charged for bribes over stake in real estate project
articles.content_orig:
Hong Kong corruption watchdog charges Zhang Yadong for taking HK$20 million in bribes from mainland Chinese developer for stake in latter’s project
Hong Kong’s corruption watchdog has charged the former head of a listed company for allegedly accepting HK$20 million (US$2.5 million) in bribes from a mainland Chinese property developer in exchange for acquiring a stake in the developer’s real estate project.
Zhang Yadong, 58, who was chairman of Greentown China Holdings from 2019 to 2025, faced a count of conspiracy to accept advantages, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said on Friday.
The case was mentioned at Eastern Court on Friday.
Prosecutors alleged that between January 2020 and March 2023, Zhang conspired with his son, a middleman, a shareholder of an estate developer in Dailian, Liaoning province, and others to accept bribes totalling HK$20 million from the shareholder in exchange for Greentown China acquiring equity interests in the developer’s project.

articles.title_orig: Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport as airlines suspend flights to Saudi capital
articles.title_zh: Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport as airlines suspend flights to Saudi capital
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has not commented on claims, but confirmed three killed in airport strikes earlier this week
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh ⁠airport with a ballistic missile, badly damaging a plane and leading some airlines to suspend flights to the capital.
The group provided no evidence, and Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the claim.
However, three people briefed on the matter told Reuters that shrapnel from ​an interception or another projectile left a Saudia Airlines commercial plane heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at a terminal on Thursday.
They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the ⁠time but they could not rule out any injuries.
Witnesses heard explosions in Riyadh, including a large blast at the King Khalid international airport. One witness told the Associated Press that fire and ambulance crews were deployed. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from the airport in a video verified by Reuters.
The witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that outgoing flights were halted, and that passengers were instructed to evacuate the airport.
Lufthansa and Air India confirmed they were ⁠suspending flights to Riyadh. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from the airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT on Thursday, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports.
It comes after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the country’s southwest.
The Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and warning workers to stay away from ⁠energy plants, which would be targeted.
Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in ​Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to ‌take back territory from the Houthis.
The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the country’s south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.
Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.
Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

articles.content_orig:
Beijing could leverage the yuan’s low interest rate to increase the currency’s worldwide use, an expert says
The 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.22 per cent on Thursday, compared with 1.69 per cent for Chinese government bonds on their first trading day after the National Day holiday – a gap of about 3.5 percentage points, compared with a record 3.7 percentage points on September 9.
Jiang Zhenlong, an associate research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Finance and Banking, argued that higher US yields weaken the appeal of yuan assets and add pressure on the exchange rate and capital flows, but also raise dollar funding costs.
“The China-US yield inversion presents an asymmetric effect: pressure on the asset allocation side and benefit on the financing side,” he wrote in the latest issue of China Money Market, a central bank-affiliated magazine.

articles.title_orig: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.title_zh: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.content_orig:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii News Now interviewed U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda and state Sen. Brenton Awa, candidates for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District, about the Iran war, aid to Israel and immigration enforcement.
Awa said he is seeking only one term in Congress.
“I only want to go for two years, one term, and the reason is, is because I don’t care about all of those world policies and all the votes that’ll have to be taken. I’ll have to care when I am taking it,” Awa said.
Awa said he wants money spent on the Iran war and support for Israel to instead go to American families dealing with disaster.
“But my biggest focus, if we’re going to send billions of dollars to Israel or another country, my only concern is why isn’t that money coming to Hawaii,” Awa said.
Tokuda said ending the war is the best way to reduce energy costs. She opposes aid to Israel because of its treatment of Palestinians.
“It’s a genocide,” Tokuda said.
“When you take a look at the weapons they are using, it was our weapons, which is why I voted against funding weapons sales to Israel for now, because that is blood on our hands,” Tokuda said.
On immigration enforcement, Awa does not oppose mass deportation but said he believes ICE has been too violent.
“The idea is good. The way they go and carry it out, and I don’t know,” Awa said. “I’m not there on the ground, so I don’t know, but other than what I see, through you guys, the media. But when you see people dying, there is no way that that should ever happen.”
Tokuda said there will be pressure to fix immigration laws after the election.
“We absolutely have to pass some kind of meaningful bipartisan immigration reform that protects our borders, that creates legal pathways to citizenship and doesn’t result in Americans getting executed in our streets,” Tokuda said.
Awa acknowledges the odds are stacked against him in a district that has never elected a Republican, and GOP voters have been discouraged by President Trump’s unpopularity.
Awa did not have to give up his Senate seat to run for Congress and has two years remaining on his term.

articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures edged higher early Friday after an underwhelming revenue report from OpenAI took some steam out of the high-flying artificial intelligence trade.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.3%, while Nasdaq 100 futures added 0.49%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 105 points, or 0.2%.
In Asia on Friday, Japan's Nikkei 225 lost over 1%, while the Topix was down 0.2%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.37%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was up 0.7%, while mainland China's CSI 300 was 0.48% lower.
Shares of SpaceX rose 2% in extended trading after the rocket company announced a deal to buy a nationwide spectrum portfolio. Shares of AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile slid as investors wondered worried the agreement could drive up competition.
AI stocks dropped on Thursday after CNBC confirmed that OpenAI told investors that it saw $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September. A $68 billion figure was widely reported last month, though a person familiar with the matter said it also included gross revenue from partners.
CoreWeave fell more than 7%, while Oracle , Intel and Super Micro Computer all lost around 5%. Advanced Micro Device slid close to 4%, while Nvidia shed almost 3%.
"If we have a number of days like this ... we could see a real rout in AI-related names," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group, on CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime." "That could sour investors."
The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 1%, marking its biggest one-day loss since mid August. Thursday marked the second down day in a row for the tech-heavy index after it climbed to fresh all-time records earlier in the week.
Tech's troubles dragged down the S&P 500 to a 0.5% loss, marking its second straight day in the red. But the blue-chip Dow bucked the downtrend, with the 30-stock index ending the session slightly above flat.
The Dow and Nasdaq Composite are both around flat week to date. The broad S&P 500 is on track for a gain of 0.6% for the week.
Investors will monitor Delta Air Lines earnings before the bell on Friday. Consumer sentiment data for October is also expected in the morning.
U.S. Treasury yields were largely stable on Friday, with the benchmark 10-year yield falling less than one basis point to 5.227%, while the 30-year yield was little changed at 5.608%.
Both remained near multi-decade highs amid concerns over persistent inflation and elevated government borrowing.
Swiss private bank UBP raised its estimated fair-value range for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.75%–5.25% in its October outlook, citing renewed inflationary pressures. The bank said in a note on Friday that risks to yields had become more balanced, although visibility remained limited, prompting it to maintain a neutral duration stance of four years and favor income from bond holdings rather than taking directional bets on interest rates.
UBP also expects the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy gradually, with rate cuts unlikely before the second half of 2027.
Oil fell Friday as U.S. President Donald Trump's comments on Iran calmed nerves, following reports that America was considering resuming strikes against Tehran.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery dropped 0.77% to $103.48 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November declined 0.68% to $90.87 per barrel.
Trump said in a post on Truth Social the U.S. "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," and was having "productive discussions" with Iran.
"In the meantime, accelerated IEA-coordinated stock releases and greater use of alternative export routes could help limit supply pressures," said Thadeu Dos Santos, regional director at markets trading platform Infinox.
"Saudi Arabia's continued use of its restored East-West pipeline is also allowing more crude to reach international markets without relying on the Strait of Hormuz, providing some offset to the upside risks," he added.
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.
Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.
"The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added.
Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which woul have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion.
Asia-Pacific markets opened subdued on Friday.
Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.76%, while the Topix was little changed. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.37%.
Japanese tech stocks were largely lower, tracking tech stock losses in the U.S. as investors assessed OpenAI's underwhelming revenue report.
Shares of SoftBank Group declined over 6%. Chip manufacturer Advantest fell 1.81%, while Tokyo Electron lost 1.52%. Renesas Electron fell 3.5%.
South Korean markets are closed for a holiday.
Asia-Pacific markets were set for a subdued open Friday as renewed doubts over the artificial intelligence boom and lingering geopolitical tensions in the Middle East dent investor sentiment.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was set to fall at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 68,515 and 68,390 respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 69,042.11.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index stood at 23,802, higher than its last close of 23,785.79.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.44% in its first hour of trade.
South Korean markets are closed for a holiday.
U.S. technology stocks came under pressure Thursday after fresh details about OpenAI's revenue raised concerns over the artificial intelligence trade. Denting sentiment further, oil prices rose after President Donald Trump said he was not keen on making a deal with Iran to end the war.
Main Street investors have grown a lot more bullish and a lot less bearish lately, according to the latest weekly survey by the American Association of Individual Investors.
Optimism toward the six-month outlook for stocks rose to 40.3% this week, the highest since mid-July, up from 34.6% last week and above the historical average of 37.5%.
Investors describing themselves as bearish dropped to 39.0% this week from 46.5% last week and 53.3%, the highest since May 2025, just three weeks ago. Historically, bears account for 31.5% of the survey and were last below that level in January 2026.
Mom-and-pop investors who characterize themselves as neutral about the six-month outlook for stocks rose to 20.8% in the latest week, from 18.9% last week.  The historical average is 31.0%.
SpaceX shares rose almost 3% in extended trading on Thursday after the rocket company unveiled an agreement to buy a nationwide spectrum portfolio.
Shares of AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile tumbled as traders worried that they could lose market share as competition rises.
— Alex Harring, Lora Kolodny

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.
In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said.
"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.
The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said.
Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.
They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".
Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.
Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.
Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.

articles.title_orig: ICE officer shoots man in vehicle in Marble Hill, Manhattan
articles.title_zh: ICE officer shoots man in vehicle in Marble Hill, Manhattan
articles.content_orig:
Man was taken to hospital where he is conscious and receiving medical attention
MARBLE HILL, Manhattan (WABC) -- A targeted ICE enforcement operation in Manhattan's Marble Hill neighborhood ended in gunfire Thursday afternoon, leaving a suspect wounded and a 5-year-old boy unharmed, according to officials, and sparking widespread condemnation from local lawmakers and immigration activists.
The shooting happened around 4 p.m. near Marble Hill Avenue and West 225th Street. City officials said an ICE agent fired multiple rounds through the front windshield of the suspect's Honda CRV. Officials said a man was in the vehicle and a child, believed to be his son, was in the back seat.
At the time of the shooting, ICE agents were attempting to detain a person being investigated for ties to migrants involved in the shooting of an off-duty customs officer in Fort Washington Park in July 2025.
Two Dominican nationals involved in the case were sentenced in federal court earlier this week, while state charges are still pending.
The Department of Homeland Security later said in a statement that ICE officers were conducting "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession. He has associations with the Trinitarios gang, the same gang that brutally killed a CBP officer last year."
During a news conference late Thursday night, NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch said at least one ICE officer discharged their weapon seven times, striking the 28-year-old driver in the neck below their left ear.
Responding NYPD officers noticed the ICE agents, and the suspect handcuffed on the ground. Officers then put the suspect in an NYPD vehicle and administered aid. He was taken to NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital, where he is in stable condition, according to Tisch. The NYPD located the child safe and is in the care of a family member.
At the same new conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that driver was later taken into ICE custody. The mayor said he spent hours on the phone with President Donald Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, negotiating the release of the man, which he says proved unsuccessful.
He condemned the ICE shooting, and called for ICE to be abolished in the city.
"We will not normalize ICE's viciousness. We will not accept its cruelty," Mamdani said. "We know — and I have said this directly, whether to the president or the public — ICE undermines public safety. It makes us less safe. This is an agency that must be abolished."
Witnesses described panic and chaos after gunfire erupted and ICE agents flooded the area.
"Like pow pow pow pow pow," witness Jeffrey said.
"It was really quick. It was boom boom boom. It was really quick," witness Marcelo Desa said.
Witnesses said the streets were crowded at the time, with children leaving school and commuters coming through the area.
"The streets were full of children coming out of school. People coming out of the bus. We were all turning the corner when shots rang out. We heard seven, eight shots really loud," one witness said.
Video from the scene captured the sound of sirens and showed a man lying in the street after being pulled from a vehicle. Witnesses described seeing what they believed was a semi-automatic assault rifle.
"Got a AR bro look at this. That's ICE. This is ICE bro," a bystander said in video recorded at the scene.
"It was a big assault rifle. It was pow pow pow pow," another witness said.
One witness said, "He shot into the back of a vehicle without knowing that there was a 5-year-old child inside the car."
Witnesses said the child was frozen in terror.
Witnesses said the heavy law-enforcement presence remained in the area well after the shooting. About 90 minutes after the shooting, dozens of ICE agents were seen leaving the scene.
"There was hundreds of kids out here. We have a huge school right here that has thousands of kids inside," one witness said.
ICE recently set a daily target of 3,000 arrests per day nationally, up from 2,000, sources told ABC News, a report which the Department of Homeland Security denied.
Hundreds of protesters gathered Thursday evening at a hospital in Inwood where the man who was shot is being treated for his injuries.
In addition to Mamdani, the shooting also sparked swift reaction from local politicians like Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Gov. Hochul is calling for "full transparency" from federal authorities, and also said she spoke with the president and DHS Secretary Mullin, urging them to "halt ICE enforcement operations in New York," and release body camera footage of the shooting to the public.
Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, who attended a press conference hosted by the New York Immigration Coalition, released a statement saying he hears the fear anger of the Marble Hill community, and also "hear their resolve, their commitment to stand by our immigrant neighbors under attack."
He added, "They belong in our city - ICE does not."
The shooting has also prompted responses from city immigration activists.
"ICE's violent tactics are a clear danger to all New Yorkers, as today's shooting in a residential neighborhood demonstrates. This incident is another reminder of the unchecked, rampant violence ICE has been spreading throughout our communities," said Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition.

articles.title_orig: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.title_zh: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.content_orig:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.
Happy World Octopus Day!  Every Oct 8, the world celebrates one of the more unusual creatures of the sea. Octopuses are well-known for their eight legs and ability to squirt ink when frightened. They’ve also been known to use tools, a sign of intelligence, and can shape-shift to mimic the colors and texture of their surroundings, an effective way to disappear from both predators and prey.
Mongabay has reported on several octopus discoveries this year, including:
Ancient octopus were apex predators
Modern colossal squid are believed to be the largest invertebrates in the sea, but Mongabay’s Shanna Hanbury recently reported on an even larger ancient octopus species whose fossils were described by Japanese researchers in April 2026.
The Japanese team found a fossilized jawbone from the now-extinct Nanaimoteuthis haggarti. Based on its jaw size, researchers suggest the octopus may have reached 6.6 to 18.6 meters (22 to 61 feet) in length. On the higher end, that’s around two-thirds the size of an adult blue whale, the largest animal to ever exist.
“It suggests that it may have been among the largest invertebrates ever known,” study co-author Yasuhiro Iba, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University in Japan, told Mongabay by email.
They were likely gigantic predators that roamed the late Cretaceous seas between 100 million to 72 million years ago.
A rare look at baby octopuses
From long dead octopus to newly born, Hanbury also reported on baby Argentine octopuses and a rare photo of them.
Patagonian octopus eggs in Puerto Lobos Protected Natural Area in Argentina. Image courtesy of Martin Brogger.
These eggs belong to a small Patagonian octopus ( Octopus tehuelchus ). It’s one of the more common octopus species in the region, but researchers still haven’t been able to determine its global conservation status, although reported catches in Patagonia have declined over the past 50 years.
The black dots inside each egg are the developing eyes of the embryos, indicating that they’re progressing toward hatching. The female octopus of this species often lays her eggs in the shell of an oyster , then guards them fiercely. She even stops eating during this period.
New octopus species are described often , including a blue octopus about the size of a golf ball recently discovered in the Galapagos.
On a deep-sea expedition in 2015, scientists used a remotely operated vehicle to find a golf-ball sized, short-armed blue octopus. In a recent study , they confirmed that it’s new to science, reported Mongabay’s David Brown.
However, questions remain about how the new species, Microeledone galapagensis , makes use of its stubby arms.
“If you gather prey by moving your arms through the sediment (as we think they do), wouldn’t it be better to have longer arms with more suckers than short little arms?” queried lead author Janet Voight.
Banner image: Big blue octopus ( Octopus cyanea ) with a diver in background. Image courtesy of David Fleetham/WWF via naturepl.com.
What does it take to turn one of the world’s richest iron deposits into a global export hub? Eastern Guinea has become a focal point in the global race for high-grade iron ore. articles.title_zh: How quickly is China learning from the Ukraine war’s latest drone tactics?
articles.content_orig:
Beijing’s effort is the most systematic of any outside power, but it faces limits learning from a war it is not fighting
But it usually took a year or more before those lessons showed up publicly in People’s Liberation Army (PLA) training, equipment or force structure, Lilly Min-Chen Lee and Kateryna Bondar wrote in a commentary published on October 7 by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The lessons drawn by China go beyond immediate tactics. Chinese analysts have also looked at the economics of mass-produced drones, ways to shorten the kill chain, fibre-optic first-person-view (FPV) drones that are harder to jam, and multiple layers of defence against sea and aerial drones.

articles.title_orig: First Georgia Senate debate spotlights fight over Trump- and Biden-era policies
articles.title_zh: First Georgia Senate debate spotlights fight over Trump- and Biden-era policies
articles.content_orig:
It was debate night in Georgia, but President Donald Trump and former President Joe Biden seemed to be onstage.
Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins squared off Thursday in the first debate in this nationally consequential Senate race, with both trying to hit the other for policies implemented by the current and former presidents.
Ossoff repeatedly asked why Collins supported tariffs that have been a key factor in the rise in the cost of consumer goods that has kept Trump’s approval ratings at historically low levels, a question Collins never directly answered.
“Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs,” Ossoff said after having already asked about Trump’s tariff regime several times.
Collins spent the hourlong debate, hosted by WANF-TV of Atlanta, not directly answering questions about the unpopular war in Iran or Trump’s economy but rather trying to saddle Ossoff with votes he took during the Biden administration to make the case that Biden is the reason for the current state of inflation and high prices.
“That Bidenomics, that Green New Deal my opponent voted for, that’s where this inflation came from,” Collins said.
The debate was broken up into four segments, but each was dominated in some form by the economy and consumer prices, topics that an NBC News poll showed are the most important issues on voters’ minds in the lead-up to Election Day.
Collins voted to support the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill, the biggest legislative achievement of Trump’s second term. The bill included provisions including no taxes on tips for hospitality workers and Social Security, which are regular midterm talking points for Republicans. But Democrats have consistently highlighted how the sweeping tax proposal disproportionately benefits the wealthy and increased the federal deficit by $1.4 trillion.
“Tax cuts are the answer to keeping more money in people’s pockets,” Collins said. “That creates ... more tax-paying people, and businesses grow.”
As Trump’s approval rating has tanked, helping Democrats overcome the GOP’s huge national financial advantage, Republican candidates across the country have distanced themselves from him on key policies ranging from tariffs to the war in Iran. Collins, however, has not been among them, keeping his place as one of Trump’s staunchest allies in key midterm Senate races.
Ossoff pressed Collins several times about why he supports Trump policies on the economy and foreign affairs.
He did say Trump’s tariffs make things “fair” in the context of trade with China and helping Georgia’s ports, which are key to the state’s economy.
“Savannah port and Brunswick port have been on my mind,” he said, without offering specifics about how the tariffs have helped them.
Pressed about the Iran war, which is increasingly unpopular , Collins defended Trump’s decision to begin bombing raids with Israel in February.
“The president had every right to make sure Iran does not get a nuclear weapon. Jon Ossoff knows this,” he said.
Ossoff has also regularly attacked Collins for continuing to support Trump’s insistence, without proof, that the 2020 presidential election was stolen, an issue that also took center stage during the debate.
“Mike Collins and Donald Trump, they are still obsessed with overturning the 2020 election,” Ossoff said.
Collins did not back down from the idea the 2020 election was stolen but focused on GOP election measures and saying Ossoff opposes the SAVE Act , a Trump-backed bill that, among other things, would require proof of citizenship to register to vote.
“Voters need confidence,” Collins said. “We live in the best country in the world, and no reason we should not have the most secure elections in the world.”
The bill has been passed in the House, but it has not had enough support in the GOP-led Senate.
Each candidate also tried to frame the other as scandal-plagued.
Ossoff hit Collins over a series of social media posts in which his son-in-law promoted white nationalist posts .
“Imagine running for the U.S. Senate while neo-Nazi propaganda is disseminated to an audience of millions from your house,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins is a bigot.”
Collins said he does not support racism or antisemitism, and he said he has told his family that.
“I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that,” Collins said of his son-in-law.
In contrast, Collins said billionaire Reid Hoffman, whose name appeared in the Epstein files , is an Ossoff donor.
“Billionaire Reid Hoffman, also one of Epstein’s buddies out there, has funneled money into his campaign,” Collins said.
Authorities have not accused Hoffman of wrongdoing in connection with Epstein. Hoffman has said he regrets having associated with Epstein.
Ossoff has been the subject of significant national speculation about whether he wants to run for president in 2028, which he has said he has “no interest” in, but that has not kept him off early shortlists.
That idea is bolstered by the fact that $50 million of the more than $100 million he has raised is from so-called small-dollar donors, which are relatively small contributions typically raised through email and other digital means from supporters across the country. An ability to digitally raise money at that clip is generally a sign of a candidate’s national name identification and support among the party’s most intense base voters, who often play an outsize role in helping choose presidential nominees.
Collins has raised more than $7 million for his campaign, according to the most recent campaign finance reports, and he has gotten his biggest boost, $25 million, from the Senate Leadership Fund, a national group that supports GOP Senate candidates.
At the beginning of the 2026 midterm cycle, the Georgia contest was seen as likely to be one of the closest in the country and a key component for Republicans as they try to hold on to their slim majority in the Senate.
The race, however, has slowly trended Ossoff’s way. Most public polling has him with a sizable lead, including a YouGov poll released last month that had him topping Collins by 10 percentage points. The poll, which has a margin of error of 2.7 percentage points, was conducted Sept. 15-18.
Georgia is still seen as a key midterm Senate battleground contest, but many Republicans see it slipping away and are focusing on other states, like Texas, Maine, North Carolina and Alaska, to try to maintain control of the Senate.
Each candidate used his finishing remarks to attack the other.
Ossoff said Collins, who runs a trucking company started by his father, a former congressman, misleads about his professional record.
“Mike has called himself a trucker,” Ossoff said. “This is a congressman’s son who inherited a seat in Congress.”
Collins got the final word, once again hitting Ossoff for voting on Biden-era policies.
“We still have not heard why Jon Ossoff votes the way he does,” Collins said. “Why he voted against our farmers ... why he voted against hardworking Georgians out there.”
Matt Dixon is a senior national politics reporter for NBC News, based in Florida.

articles.title_orig: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
articles.title_zh: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
articles.content_orig:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping.
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity.
Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs.
Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks.
“I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point.
Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election.
Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist.
The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly .
“I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.”
Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise.
“It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.”
At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.”
Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump.
New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war .
“I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.”
El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households.
“Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.”
El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”
The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.”
“I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.”
El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer.
“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied.
“We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.”
The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts , with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game.
Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith .
Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed . And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.”
Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name.
“Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.”
He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.”
Henry J. Gomez is a senior national political reporter for NBC News

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Suspends Microsoft From Green Card Program, Alleging Visa Fraud
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Suspends Microsoft From Green Card Program, Alleging Visa Fraud
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification program on Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said, as the Trump administration continues to take aim at immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of November's midterm elections.
Sonderling said the Labor Department won't accept or process any new applications under the program for a host of companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL.
The secretary said Adobe and Microsoft were also suspended "due to multiple active federal investigations."
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said.
Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft specifically, pointing to the firm's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed that the company "replaced" those workers with people on H-1B visas.
"So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said.
Microsoft responded to Vance's claims and defended its hiring practices in a statement Thursday, saying "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees," the company said.
President Donald Trump is set to award the National Medal of Science to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other leading technology CEOs on Thursday at the same summit where the suspension announcement was made.
Nadella is from India and moved to the U.S. in 1988. He joined Microsoft in 1992.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su are also being honored at Thursday's medal ceremony. Each of the leaders immigrated to the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa and Su and Huang were born in Taiwan.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk," Vance said. "I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that."
Tech giants like Microsoft, Google , Amazon and Apple have been among the top sponsors of H-1B visas for decades. This year, Amazon had the highest number of petitions at 35,426 workers, followed by Cognizant and EY, according to 2026 data from Levels.fyi .
Microsoft was a close fourth at 21,706 petitions for 2026, with a median base salary of $180,710.
Microsoft said that petitions were only filed for workers "who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and said Microsoft's wages for H-1B workers were among the highest of all H-1B filings.
CNBC has reached out to Adobe for comment.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia-Backed Firmus IPO Collapses as AI Valuation Concerns Grow
articles.title_zh: Nvidia-Backed Firmus IPO Collapses as AI Valuation Concerns Grow
articles.content_orig:
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.
Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.
"The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added.
Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which woul have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion.
In August, the company announced a $2 billion funding round backed by Nvidia, Coatue Management, Blackstone and Jane Street, bringing its total equity raised over the preceding year to more than $3 billion and its valuation to over $10.5 billion.
Firmus also announced agreements with Meta last month to provide GPU computing capacity at its AI data centers in Southeast Asia, built on Nvidia's DSX platform, to support Meta's AI research, model development and training.

articles.title_orig: Open Door Mission hosts 24-hour 'Conversations on a Bench' for World Homeless Day
articles.title_zh: Open Door Mission hosts 24-hour 'Conversations on a Bench' for World Homeless Day
articles.content_orig:
Rochester, N.Y. — This Saturday will mark World Homeless Day, and the Open Door Mission is raising awareness.
Thursday, it's participating in "Conversations on a Bench", a 24-hour livestream event.
Ministry CEO’s will spend 24 hours sitting on a bench engaging in conversations with anyone who stops by.
The idea is to re-humanize homelessness and amplify stories of hope and transformation.
"There are many, many reasons why homelessness comes about," said Open Door Mission CEO Robert Williams. "Here in Rochester, two of the primary drivers are addiction and mental illness."
He added, "I am celebrating 19 years of recovery. I went through a 25-year addiction. So I walked that path, and I sit here now as the CEO of the open door mission because there was something that was called hope."
The conversations continue at the corner of Plymouth Avenue and Main Street through 3 p.m. Friday.

articles.title_orig: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.title_zh: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.content_orig:
Sailors wave aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier as it returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
CORONADO, Calif. — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.
The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.
Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
"It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off."
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.
"It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday."
She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.
Family and friends cheer as the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
"It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said.
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."
Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
"She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
"I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Karl Anderson/AP hide caption
Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.
He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.
The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed nearly 3,700 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.title_zh: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The world’s largest wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills is barreling toward a Dec. 2 completion date . Perhaps the only thing that could stop it is a fierce winter storm.
Already, a concrete bridge stretches across 10 lanes of whizzing traffic. Atop that, there’s a lush landscape sewn with 6,000 native plants. Recently, crews completed another overpass over adjacent Agoura Road. A big remaining to-do is to fill in the gap between the freeway and the road — and the freeway to the land to the north — with millions of cubic feet of soil to create a seamless pathway for animals.
The idea behind the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is to provide a lifeline for mountain lions in the Santa Monica Mountains, locked in by traffic and suffering from the effects of inbreeding.
“We’re just hoping El Niño ‘s on our side,” said Beth Pratt, president of the Wildlife Crossing Fund and public face of the project. “I keep saying, ‘Mother Nature, we’re trying to help you. Let’s not throw any more complications our way.” A super-sized version of the climate pattern is looming, and there’s a good chance Southern California could be doused.
Some rain is not a big deal but flooding would shut down work for safety reasons. At a final construction update held near the crossing Thursday, Robert Rock, lead landscape architect and principal designer for the crossing, explained that the soil in the area is rich in clay and silt. When wet, it gets dangerously slick and slippery.
Heavy precipitation can also derail the soil compaction process, where crews lay down the soil in layers and go over each with a construction vehicle known as a roller. In the distance, workers were busy doing just that as the fierce late morning sun beat down.
“If you’re trying to compact a mud puddle, it wouldn’t really compact, right?” he said at a trailhead off of Agoura Road. “Because if you push that down, the mud just [splats] in either direction.”
In fact, something like that happened amid historic rains in the winter of 2022-23. Construction workers were busy preparing to pour the concrete for the bottom layer of the north wall. But water collected in the trench that was dug for it as they were working to compact the soil.
That pushed back the original completion date of late 2025. Right-wing pundits and politicos in recent months have attacked the project over the delays and a high price tag that’s currently $114 million. A March post in an outlet published by a conservative think tank called it a “bridge to nowhere” and “jobs program for environmentalists.” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy compared it with the state’s long-delayed, budget-busting high-speed train.
Around the time the outrage reached a fever pitch, however, the completion date was announced.
Pratt said “the hate” has worn on her. She’s been called a “fraud,” “retard” and worse, and she’s even afraid to post about the crossing on social media. “Of course we’re still going to celebrate” at the finish line, she said.
At stake is the survival of the Santa Monica Mountains’ isolated, beleaguered mountain lion population, which is listed as threatened. Seth Riley, wildlife branch chief for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, said 41% of documented matings were between close relatives since 2002, the start of an ongoing study of mountain lions in and around the Santa Monicas.
Just a few months ago, the National Park Service caught a young collared male at the western end of the mountain range who had a kinked tail — a sign of inbreeding. It’s not the first such documented deformity but shows the problems persist, Riley said. If the situation gets to the point where their reproduction is affected, modeling has shown there’s “essentially a 100% chance of extinction” within 50 years, he added.
But he doesn’t think it’s too late. The soon-to-open crossing will let the big cats seek mates in the Simi Hills and beyond — and allow fresh blood to travel into their neck of the woods, he said. Genetic diversity is expected to go up, though not overnight.
In the last three weeks, a trail camera stationed close to the south end of the crossing has captured coyotes, deer, a female lion with two big cubs — even as construction churns on next door, said Jeff Sikich, a wildlife biologist at the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
Recently, in the Simi Hills north of the crossing, his team marked three kittens, the first litter for the 3 ½-year-old lion known as P-113.
“These kittens might be — once they grow up and leave mom at roughly around 1½ — one of the first lions to actually use the wildlife crossing,” he said.

Since joining The Times in 2020, she has investigated mental health policy and jumped on breaking news. Reggie Bush was the face of USC football’s glory years — and one of the figures at the center of its collapse. But behind the saga was a group of men trying to build a sports agency around Bush, and in the process, said they provided him and his family with the benefits that would ultimately bring the NCAA down on USC.
