articles.title_zh: Sony’s new USB-C spatial mic captures the world around you without capturing you in wires
articles.content_orig:
We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›
Sony spent 2026 releasing tons of top-notch playback products, from Bluetooth headphones to DJ-friendly party speakers to surprisingly affordable pro IEMs . Now the Japanese giant introduces something to capture immersive content you can play on all those audio accessories. The ECM-AX10 is a compact USB-C microphone for vloggers, mobile filmmakers, and content creators, and the world’s first Eclipsa Audio -certified mic for smartphones .
Featuring four omnidirectional capsules, the ECM-AX10 can record Ambisonics, binaural, and stereo. This lets you capture the sense of space, direction, and distance appropriate for the project/format, whether it’s travel reels or festival feels, sports cheers or reviewing gear.
Ambisonics’s four-channel 48 kHz/32-bit float capabilities, plus Sony’s Spatial Audio Video Tool, mean you can publish a full-sphere Eclipsa Audio experience on YouTube, based on the open IAMF (Immersive Audio Model and Format) standard. The Binaural recording’s two channels of that 48 kHz/16-, 24-, or 32-bit quality can be translated to 360 Reality Audio for headphone-optimized 3D rendering. And stereo is, well, stereo. You know it, you love it, you want some more of it. It makes the microphone compatible with general recording and video apps and whatever social channel you prefer.
As for the package these containers come in, the ECM-AX10 is 24g, has a Selfie Mode for rear or front-facing alignment, includes an attenuator (ATT) switch that drops sensitivity -20dBFS to avoid overloading (plus additional Noise Cut controls), features a 3-axis gyroscope and 3-axis accelerometer to keep audio aligned with the video’s orientation, and offers a 3.5mm minijack for wired monitoring (a great opportunity to try those Sony IER-M500 IEMs, or others ). There’s also a windscreen; spacer sheet; shoe-mount microphone holder (Cold shoe / No electrical contacts); and USB-C extension cable in the package.
Thanks to the ECM-AX10, you don’t have to risk your $15,000 C-800G to capture engaging, expressive, like you were there ambiance.

articles.title_orig: In a world where the glamour of evil rules, Catholics must create beauty
articles.title_zh: In a world where the glamour of evil rules, Catholics must create beauty
articles.content_orig:
Think of a moment when you felt God’s nearness. And I mean felt, not as something you could explain or argue, but as a closeness that reached into the depth of your being in ways you could barely describe—and yet you knew.
My son had one of those experiences. He was on a work trip to Mexico City and took an afternoon to join a tour of the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe. He was rushed and distracted, so he decided to return later on his own. On a long-distance video call that evening, his eyes wide with wonder, he described the experience. He was sitting quietly before the image of La Virgen preserved on Juan Diego’s tilma high above the main altar when, suddenly, he “knew” he was not alone. And then it hit him all at once that he was never alone. He felt La Virgen’s loving gaze fixed intently on him and became aware that my late mother (his beloved Abi) was sitting next to him in the pew, “like every time we went to Misa together when I was little.”
The whole experience felt familiar and natural; being there with a community in prayer was being en familia. In the beauty of that moment, he discovered that heaven and earth were not separate realities but instead one. My son was changed by that moment. In a world steeped in materialist cynicism, where our young struggle with disillusionment and despair, he had an experience of beauty so profound that it generated hope in him, a hope that keeps renewing itself. When his little blind dog was sick recently, he hung a small medal of La Virgen from his collar. God’s compassion knows no limits.
Maybe you have had such an experience of beauty. I hope so, because you also represent hope.
The experience my son had was not a private revelation but the fruit of a community—the loving work of generations who recognize the primal human need for beauty and continue to labor to make it perceptible. He benefited from artists and architects who envision ways to help us feel the power of beauty. He kept in his heart the stories that mothers and grandmothers recount of God’s loving presence. Most of all, he received the gift that countless communities of faith generously bestow on one another—the witness to being grafted into a larger story and the renewal this brings from generation to generation. This recognition and expansion of beauty as heaven’s solidarity with us has been central to the Christian faith from its very beginnings.
St. John Paul II, in his pastoral “ Letter to Artists ,” in a section titled “The ‘Beauty’ That Saves,” writes: “Faced with the sacredness of life and of the human person, and before the marvels of the universe, wonder is the only appropriate attitude.” The Christian imagination is that quality that allows us to push against the boundaries and apparent inevitability of an often painful what is into the possibility and healing of what could be by the light of our religious tradition. For Christians, this open possibility is the source of our hope in God’s reign, which is both here and not yet here. The reign is both breaking in and incomplete as it pulls us toward its fulfillment. The reign requires imagination, commitment and experiences of it, perceptible in beauty, to nourish it. The invitation to imagine expansively and the work of cultivating ways to do this are central to a faith that engages with the realities of this world and responds to the “ signs of the times, ” as the Second Vatican Council emphasized.
Our theologies, the ways we speak of God and our relationship to God and to one another, must begin with what is happening around us. If we endeavor to attune ourselves to experiencing the world as it is, this will lead us through a process of interpreting and wrestling with reality. It is this process, done in community and by the light of Sacred Scripture and tradition, that blooms in an expansive imagination and can become effective action for the reign of God.
John Paul II wrote that “beauty will save the world”; in doing this he was echoing a long tradition uniting the aesthetic with the ethical. Sixteen years later, Pope Francis would also appeal to beauty as a powerful aid to building ecological solidarity, naming beauty and its effects over 40 times in his encyclical “Laudato Si ’.” He writes: “Faith allows us to interpret the meaning and the mysterious beauty of what is unfolding” in the universe. He adds that Jesus “was able to invite others to be attentive to the beauty that there is in the world because he himself was in constant touch with nature, lending it an attention full of fondness and wonder.” The insight into the power of beauty encouraged ancient thinkers to identify qualities they called the universals, or the transcendentals. These were ways of experiencing reality and evaluating it that appeared to be so fundamental that they were shared across radically diverse human groups. So how can we unite around these principles?
Understand what is good. Despite differences across cultures, humans seem to share some basic understanding of what is good. Religious codes throughout the world often converge in defining what is good and what is not. Ancient peoples understood that there were markers in the ways life unfolded that showed what would help a community flourish and markers that conversely cried out “caution” and pointed to what would hinder and thwart a community’s survival. Good was real and so was evil, and the difference between them needed to be understood and acted upon.
Embrace what is true. Humans also seem to share an ability to assess what is true and what is not. These assessments of truthfulness are not connected to our simplistic modern idea of “the factual” but rather to a more robust and profound experience, the experience of wisdom resonant in the human heart. There are truths and there are also lies; and as history painfully shows, the difference between these is vital to the survival of a community. This difference also needs to be visible, understood and acted upon.
Behold beauty. Beyond goodness and truth, the ancients identified a third “universal,” and some of us give it pride of place because it validates the other two by attracting us and pointing us toward them. This is what we call beauty, and unlike some who would claim “beauty is in the eye of the beholder,” reducing it to a purely subjective experience, those of us who argue for the transcendental power of beauty are closer to Shakespeare’s idea that “a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.” The sweetness is universally felt, universally recognized and universally delightful, regardless of what name we might give it. What’s more, in a Christian understanding, beauty and our ability to recognize and love it originate in God’s abundant generosity and communicate God’s presence with us. As John Paul II puts it, beauty “has drawn its sap precisely from the mystery of the Incarnation.” This was the experience my son had.
Find strength in unity. The strength of the transcendentals is precisely in their unity and how they bring us to union with a mystery that wants to be known. If something is good, then it is also true and most assuredly beautiful. And since beauty is perceptible through our senses and thus present in the world, it can do the work of revealing the other two. Nothing can be beautiful if it lies or leads us into evil. Because of this, beauty’s opposite—ugliness—is also a valuable and powerful ethical marker that we must be capable of recognizing and acting upon. What I want to highlight here is that the events of our present day reveal that we have neglected to cultivate our ability to see true beauty and consequently have become blind to its heartbreaking absence in ugliness. This failure is playing a critical role in what is happening in our world. What happens when we can no longer recognize beauty? What happens when ugliness is camouflaged so we cannot see it? What is the outcome of losing our ability to discern the true and the good?

articles.title_orig: DoJ seeks to charge ex-Trump aide who gave key testimony on January 6 attack
articles.title_zh: DoJ seeks to charge ex-Trump aide who gave key testimony on January 6 attack
articles.content_orig:
Cassidy Hutchinson told panel she had been told Trump lunged for wheel of SUV to try to join mob at Capitol
Prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division are seeking criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson , a former top Trump White House aide who gave explosive testimony to the committee that investigated the US attack on the Capitol, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The potential charges involve lying to Congress, the person said.
Hutchinson, a former top aide to the White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, told the panel among other things that the deputy chief of staff for operations told her that Trump did not want to return to the White House on January 6 and at one point grabbed the wheel of his SUV to try to join supporters at the Capitol. Republicans have long disputed this account.
The justice department’s efforts to indict Hutchinson were first reported by Punchbowl News on Thursday.
“The department does not confirm or deny the existence of investigations, or the lack thereof,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
In April, the New York Times reported that prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division, which handles investigations into civil rights crimes, had been tapped to investigate Hutchinson. It was seen as a highly unusual move at the time since the investigation would typically be handled by the US attorney for the district of Columbia. Hutchinson also said she was under investigation by the Department of Justice in filings in an unrelated case.
The case is the latest example of how Trump has used the justice department to prosecute his enemies. Last year, the justice department indicted former FBI director James Comey on charges of lying to Congress and Letitia James on mortgage fraud . Both indictments were dismissed after a judge ruled the prosecutor overseeing them had been unlawfully appointed. The department has since filed a new indictment against Comey for posting a picture of seashells arranged in a formation that said “8647.”

The Trump justice department has also filed charges against the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center and the journalist Don Lemon.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Judge hears CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s request on Trump’s press ban
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Judge hears CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s request on Trump’s press ban
articles.content_orig:
• A federal judge briefly extended CNN, MS Now, and Politico’s access to the White House while he considers a longer-term ruling on President Donald Trump’s press ban. US District Judge Timothy Kelly signaled skepticism about the administration’s arguments for allowing the ban.
• The Justice Department argued that Trump previously put “CNN on notice” with his complaints about “fake news,” adding: “Trump doesn’t mind negative press stories if he deserves them.”
• Lawyers for the news organizations said this week that the White House had offered no new evidence to support its repeated claims that the news outlets’ reporting has endangered national security. On Thursday, attorney Ted Boutros Jr. told the judge that national security reporting is important to “hold the government accountable.” Outlets, he said, take national security concerns into consideration ahead of publication if raised by the government.
Our live coverage of today’s hearing has concluded. Please scroll through the posts below to learn about all that happened in court. You can read our takeaways here.
Judge Tim Kelly expressed skepticism about the government’s arguments to end his temporary restraining order and allow the enforcement of the White House media ban.
Kelly repeatedly noted to the Justice Department attorney that he was bound by DC Circuit precedent — including the precedent that the administration was objecting to.
One line of question for government lawyer Michael Velchik was focused the lack of notice the outlets received before the White House cut off their access. The case law around due process claims — one of the key claims the outlets are making in this case — says that only in “hair on fire” situations can the government yank away a right it has granted a person without given them advanced notice, Kelly said, emphasizing a requirement that the government show there was “urgent need” for taking immediate action.
The situation in this case, however, seemed “more attenuated,” Kelly said.
The judge also grilled Velchik on the gap between the rationale that Trump has repeatedly given for banning in outlets — Trump, in repeated, public remarks pointed to their history of negative coverage of him — and the national security justification that the Justice Department is leaning on in court filings.
Kelly said it was “unusual” that “the decision maker seems to have said …I am taking this action because ‘x’ and ‘y’,” and now the government is saying, “it’s ‘z’.”
“It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one to find” looking at other relevant cases, Kelly said, calling it an “uphill climb” for the Justice Department.
Velchik argued that the Supreme Court decision upholding Trump’s travel ban against mostly Muslim countries in his first administration supported the administration on this front.
While Kelly seemed somewhat open to the idea that the White House could ban reporters for national security reasons in some contexts, he appeared skeptical of how the administration was trying to use that justification in this case. He asked Velchik to walk him through “the strongest things in the record” that bolster the national security justification.
A federal judge is still weighing a longer term extension of his ruling blocking aspects of President Donald Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
In the interim, US District Judge Timothy Kelly extended a temporary order through Tuesday that requires the Trump administration grant those outlets entry to the White House grounds.
The judge said a ruling could come on Tuesday or earlier.
If you’re just joining us, here are key moments from today’s hearing:
CNN’s Jeremy Herb, Tierney Sneed, Holmes Lybrand and Evan Perez contributed to this report.
Judge Tim Kelly was focused on whether the First Amendment would permit a ban on a news organization for publishing false information. His first line of questioning for CNN attorney Ted Boutrous was about disentangling the White House’s allegations that outlets’ “reporting was false” versus reporting that administration was thought was “not positive for the president.”
Kelly asked whether those two concepts should be viewed the same way under First Amendment law — noting it was “very hard to pull apart” the claims.
Boutrous said both allegations would still amount to viewpoint discrimination. He said that even falsity was a “debatable” issue, particularly if a president claimed that “what you’re saying is false because I don’t like it.”
Kelly pushed on the distinction harder. It may be hard to establish objective falsity if one was reporting that “the vibes were bad” at an event, Kelly noted – a reference to one of the stories the White House citied to justify the ban.
But the judge asked about a journalist who reported the sky was red instead of blue. Boutrous said that scenario was a “closer call” and he emphasized that the stories cited in this case were not anything like that. The attorney warned of “unbridled discrimination” if the administration was able to just declare that a story was false.
Ted Boutros, a lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico, told reporters outside US District Court in Washington, DC, that Judge Tim Kelly said to expect a ruling by Tuesday, if not before.
Kelly said in court that he was still weighing a longer-term extension of his ruling blocking aspects of President Donald Trump’s White House of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
In the meantime, Kelly briefly extended a temporary order through Tuesday that requires the Trump administration grant those outlets entry to the White House grounds.
In his questioning of the lawyer for the news organizations, Judge Timothy Kelly said he “was struck” by the outlets arguments in their briefing that the First Amendment protects the publication of classified information.
He asked if the government could take action similar to Trump’s press ban in a scenario where a reporter published classified information that is shown to be “very harmful” to the national security.
Media attorney Ted Boutrous said drawing a line there “would be a very dangerous road to go down” and that a ban for publishing classified information would still be content-based, in violation of the First Amendment.
A federal judge said at the end of a hearing Thursday that he was still weighing whether to extend his ruling blocking aspects of President Donald Trump’s White House ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly, however, extended a temporary order through Tuesday that requires the Trump administration grant those outlets entry to the White House grounds.
Attorney for CNN, MS NOW and Politico Ted Boutrous Jr. reiterated the subjective nature of the White House ban against media outlets and argued that it was President Donald Trump’s decision.
“We know what he decided. He said it over and over again,” Boutrous said. “He issued the ban himself.”
He argued that “the only thing I can come up with” is that the president likely “woke up on the wrong side of the bed” and decided to issue the ban.
Boutrous said that the president has said that he doesn’t like scrutiny of his policies, which points to viewpoint discrimination.
Earlier, Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik argued that it’s “within the discretion of the president” to remove reporters or news outlets from the White House.
Velchik said “CNN has been on notice for years” and that Trump has long been calling the outlet “fake news.”
“Trump doesn’t mind negative press stories if he deserves them,” Velchik added.
The hearing over the attempt by the White House to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico has ended without a ruling from the bench.

articles.title_orig: Europe And China Confront Growing Trade Tensions
articles.title_zh: Europe And China Confront Growing Trade Tensions
articles.content_orig:
Europe’s top trade negotiators are meeting with Chinese officials in Beijing this Thursday and Friday, October 8th and 9th, to discuss the European Union’s growing trade deficit with China, which runs at €1 billion per day, as well as other agenda items, according to The New York Times.
Since June, the EU and China have been locked in tense trade negotiations, with the EU concerned about the overwhelming flood of Chinese imports, which, according to Politico, is putting pressure on domestic manufacturers and forcing plant closures and layoffs. “I think our Chinese partners understood that this has direct implications on the future of emblematic European companies,” Maroš Šefčovič, European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, said.
Additionally, according to Reuters, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament last month that the trade imbalance had reached a tipping point and that Europe would use all the tools at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.
The forthcoming meetings will include talks regarding China’s growing automobile export industry to Europe. Imports of plug-in hybrid automobiles into the EU have increased by 86%, with a 20% decline in prices, while imports of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) have risen by 40%, according to Reuters.
Among other items on the agenda is the renewable energy industry, specifically wind turbines, as well as Europe’s growing dependency on China for rare earth minerals and China’s increasing restrictions on their export. These minerals are crucial to the production of automobiles, drones, lasers, semiconductors, jetliners, electronics, and other advanced technologies.
As the EU and China approach a crucial turning point this week, significant economic consequences loom for both sides. For the EU, the primary concern is preventing further deindustrialisation and the potential loss of large numbers of domestic jobs. For China, the challenge lies in restructuring its economic model and reducing its reliance on exports to prevent the closure of key international markets and avoid contributing to a broader global economic crisis. While the EU is making every effort to reach a fair trade deal, as shown in its leaders’ various public statements, the disadvantages pose a notable risk. A potential trade dispute between Europe and China is not improbable and, if it occurs, could devolve into a trade war.
The success of this week’s negotiations will depend on the EU demonstrating political determination to implement concrete policies and measures to protect its economic interests. Taking such action could strengthen the EU’s negotiating position and encourage Chinese leadership to pursue a meaningful agreement, rather than risk the introduction of further measures, as noted by the Friends of Europe think tank. Ideally, a substantial trade deal could provide lasting economic benefits for both sides. Regardless of the outcome of these meetings, one thing is certain: Europe’s relationship with China is changing.

articles.title_orig: At Texas Rally, Trump and Paxton Make for an Awkward Pair
articles.title_zh: At Texas Rally, Trump and Paxton Make for an Awkward Pair
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”, and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
after newsletter promotion
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped and thinks it may have been a politically motivated attack
articles.title_zh: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped and thinks it may have been a politically motivated attack
articles.content_orig:
A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona said she was raped in August while out fixing campaign signs along a road in the Phoenix metropolitan area, and she thinks the attack may have been politically motivated.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, 52, told the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office that she was returning to her car around 2 a.m. on Aug. 14 in Sun City when she was struck in the back of the head and raped by a man, according to an incident report obtained by NBC News. She said a second man also climbed on top of her before she tried to fight him off.
Greene-Placentia, who is challenging Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, reported the alleged assault to authorities on Aug. 31, more than two weeks after she said it occurred. Greene-Placentia told police she believed her attackers recognized her as a political figure, according to the incident report.
She told NBC News on Wednesday that she recalled hearing one of the suspects saying “ick b----,” which she said in her head filled in as “democratic b----.”
“Bernadette also recalled one of the male suspects stating, ‘democratic b----,’ at some point during the incident but she did not clarify or recall when this may have been said,” the incident report states.
Greene-Placentia told NBC News that she had little memory of the moments leading up to the attack and did not hear anyone approach her. She said she was struck in the back of her head in a way that left a “huge lump.”
When she regained consciousness on the ground, she said, one man was sexually assaulting her. She said she then tried to fight off a second man.
Greene-Placentia said the second man said, “You’re right, she’s not worth it,” before they left, according to the incident report. She added that she does not recall the men’s faces or their appearances.
“I don’t know how long I laid there. I don’t think it was very long,” she said. “And then I remember looking up, I guess I had rolled over, and my car was only like 3 yards away.”
“All I can remember is their feet, their pant leg,” she later added. “It’s frustrating.”
Her campaign manager confirmed to NBC News that Greene-Placentia and others on the campaign often go out in the middle of the night to repair and put out campaign signs to avoid the heat and traffic.
Greene-Placentia said she returned home after the alleged attack but does not remember the drive. According to the incident report, she did not seek medical treatment or undergo a sexual assault forensic examination. She told police she took three showers and a bath immediately after the sexual assault.
She told NBC News she initially kept the incident to herself because she was embarrassed that she was unable to defend herself — particularly given the years she spent learning how to protect herself when she was a long-haul truck driver.
“I will tell you, I have pretty good situational awareness,” she said. “You’re not a woman in trucking without being aware of your surroundings. Somebody was pretty f---ing quiet, and they snuck up behind me and hit me on the back of the head.”
Greene-Placentia said she told her husband and communications coordinator about the assault two to three days afterward, according to the incident report. Her husband and communications coordinator recounted to the Phoenix New Times how she told them what happened.
“I never imagined that something like this would happen just, you know, miles from my house, and I was embarrassed. Like, ‘Oh my God, I couldn’t defend myself,’” she said. “So I didn’t want to tell anybody.”
Her landlord, who asked to remain anonymous out of respect for her privacy, told NBC News she encountered an “extremely shaken” Greene-Placentia a few days after the alleged incident on the driveway as she was leaving to have dinner with a friend. She recalled Greene-Placentia was “visibly trembling” and “appeared as though she might have difficulty remaining on her feet.”
“I asked her, ‘Are you OK?’ At that point, I saw her visibly compose herself and change her demeanor,” the landlord said. “She told me that she was upset about the lack of support she felt she was receiving from the Democratic Party. We had a brief conversation about that as she went into the garage to access her apartment.”
The landlord added that she remembered being struck by how shaken Greene-Placentia had appeared and did not know what was causing that reaction. She added that she does not want to speculate on her state of mind or about anything she did not personally witness.
“My concern is for Bernadette and for treating her with dignity and respect as she deals with an extraordinarily difficult experience,” she said. “I hope the focus remains on her well-being and on allowing the appropriate authorities to conduct their work.”
Greene-Placentia explained to NBC News that she eventually decided to contact authorities after delivering a campaign speech to a group of seniors and found herself reflecting on her promise to advocate for others.
“I couldn’t look people in the eye and say I’m going to fight for them if I’m not willing to fight for everybody,” she said.
Greene-Placentia said the alleged attack also left her with bruises on her back and arms, and she has what appears to be finger marks where someone gripped her. She told police she didn’t take pictures of the bump on the back of her head or bruises, the incident report states. She said that the bruises were still visible by the time she spoke to investigators, but they did not take photographs.
The Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office told NBC News on Wednesday that the investigation is ongoing. The office did not immediately respond to a request for an update or if any suspects have been identified on Thursday.
The attorney general’s office declined to comment, telling NBC News it is not involved in this investigation.
Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., responded to the news on Wednesday night, writing on X he is “heartbroken” and calling for those responsible to be held accountable. In a statement from her office, Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs said she is “outraged” by the alleged “cruel and cowardly attack, and it has no place in Arizona.”
“No one should have to fear for their safety, or the safety of the people they love, while serving their community,” the statement said. “Violence of any kind, against anyone, will not be tolerated in our state. Our hearts are with Bernadette and her loved ones.”
If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.
Liz Kreutz is an NBC News correspondent.
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Michelle Cho is a producer for "NBC Nightly News with Lester Holt."

articles.title_orig: John Bisset, Engineer and Educator, Has Died
articles.title_zh: John Bisset, Engineer and Educator, Has Died
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
John Bisset, who dedicated his career to the broadcast industry as a skilled engineer, consultant, sales executive and educator, and who authored Radio World’s popular column Workbench, has died after a period of illness. He was 73.
He spent 55 years in the industry. In his later career, Bisset served a who’s who of equipment manufacturers, including Harris Corp., Dielectric, Broadcast Electronics, Nautel, Tieline, Elenos and Telos Alliance.
[Email your thoughts about John Bisset so we can share. Send to [email protected] .]
His technical knowledge made him uniquely qualified to understand product design, but his ability to communicate, his hallmark, not only made him an asset in sales but as a teacher.
And that has been the hallmark of Workbench.
Every edition delivered hands-on, real-world engineering tips where readers learned something new. A testament to Bisset’s ability to build a vast industry network, ideas poured in from readers and contacts who wrote to him regularly.
Tips earned Society of Broadcast Engineers certification credit, again, a testament to Workbench’s standing.
“One of the fun things about this business is the long-term relationships you make, even though you may not talk to these people for years,” Bisset once wrote.
Radio World Editor in Chief Paul McLane said the column will continue, as Bisset wanted, with a new author to be announced later.
The first Workbench appeared in Radio World on Aug. 8, 1990. Bisset, who was Radio World’s technical editor at the time, began authoring the column on Nov. 7 of that year.
In his very first Workbench column, Bisset offered this piece of advice: “I’d like to encourage you to look around your plant to see what you’ve built that could help someone else. We all know of those little insignificant projects that may appear to be ‘just common sense.’ However, we’ve also all been in the position where we can’t see the forest for the trees.”
He authored approximately 920 Workbench columns over his career. Readers routinely told Radio World that Workbench was their favorite section of the publication.
Bisset told Paul McLane in 2020 that he was especially proud of the column’s popularity among programming and management readers. He understood the power of working the ladder.
“Make friends with your group’s personnel manager,” Bisset would write. “They can be an ally.”
Or, take them to your transmitter site, as Bisset once suggested in 2003. “Not only will it give them some perspective of the work you do, but you’ll earn a little more respect when they see the inside of a transmitter or phasor.”
There was, and still is, a resounding consensus among those who worked with him most of just how highly Bisset was regarded.
“He’s the same gentleman I have always known,” Marty Sacks of Telos Alliance told us in 2020. “The service he has provided to so many, including me, all these years through his Workbench columns have truly been a labor of love.”
In 2007, SBE honored Bisset with its Educator of the Year Award .
“John Bisset is an ‘engineer’s engineer,'” Frank Baptista wrote on his LinkedIn page following Bisset’s 2009 installation of an FM and HD Radio transmitter at UMass Dartmouth. “Anyone who has been a broadcast engineer for any length of time will know that he is considered one of the experts in the industry.”
He also understood his role as an advocate. A broadcast engineer, whether full-time or contract-based, is so often misunderstood. The tips and tricks included in Workbench sometimes needed the support of higher management to pull off.
“It is really important to let the people above you, the managers, the owners, know that you are taking care of their facility and are doing a good job with it,” he once told Kirk Harnack’s This Week in Radio Tech. “You’re saving the station money and you’re keeping it on the air at the same time.”
Some of the nuggets made us laugh . An almost understated simplicity was Workbench’s calling card. But every now and then, if you paid close attention, John would insert a prescient piece of wisdom that would resonate through any walk of life.
“Time. In this business, it can control us,” he wrote on May 9, 2007. “If time gets out of hand, it can destroy us.”
As a director of engineering told John early in his career : “’No radio or TV station is worth dying for.’ Your most important job is to work safely and return to your family at the end of the day.”
John often wrote in Workbench that he was fortunate to have been mentored by chief engineers as he worked his way up the ranks. Some of Bisset’s favorite memories included early AM radio improvement efforts and demonstrating Delta Electronics’ Splatter Monitor to the Federal Communications Commission with colleague Tom Wright.
Known as an accomplished chief and contract engineer, Bisset presented and moderated an all-day Radio Transmitter Workshop at the NAB Radio Show from 1997 to 2003, as well as three additional workshops at the spring NAB Show. He was also a frequent presenter at SBE Ennes Workshops around the U.S. and at chapter meetings.
Bisset co-founded Multiphase, a successful broadcast engineering service company, in 1990. He went on to serve as regional RF sales manager for Broadcast Electronics.
At Dielectric, he directed the completion of several product initiatives, including the Dielectric Pattern Viewer. During his tenure at Harris Broadcast, he earned three sales awards and sold 55 transmitters in a single year, setting a company sales record.
In a July 2018 Workbench, Bisset reflected on an early motivator of his fondness for tinkering with equipment.
“With the move by utilities to underground service distributions, you don’t see many aerial cable splicing tents anymore; but as a young boy, I watched a phone tech strap on his climbing spikes and belt and ascend the pole outside my house,” he wrote. “He assembled a platform and tent and crawled inside.
“As a little boy, I found this fascinating. I ran inside and ran a piece of string between the radiator and end table, and built a similar structure with my TinkerToys. A couple of tissues and tape completed my tent — and then I dispatched my plastic army men inside the tent to get to work.”
He was born Oct. 31, 1952 as John Paul Bisset. At age 10, he appeared on Willard Scott’s “Bozo the Clown” show in Washington, D.C. There he got his first taste of broadcasting.
John recalled going home afterward and, with the help of his father, rigging up his own version of Bozo’s TV studio, using cardboard boxes with pie tins as lights dangling from the ceiling. He used several boxes to model as television cameras, alongside empty fruit cans to serve as mock-up lenses.
As McLane detailed in a 2020 feature celebrating Workbench’s 30th anniversary , at age 12, Bisset constructed a pirate Top 40 radio station in his home, using money from his paper route to purchase equipment. He hooked a Lafayette mic mixer up to two turntables and fed a reel-to-reel deck into a Lafayette wireless AM transmitter, covering a two-block radius.
His first professional job came at age 16 at WFAX(AM) in northern Virginia, serving the Washington market.
“Program Director Roy Martin hired me as a summer relief announcer when I was 16,” Bisset recalled. “I worked there part-time through high school and college, and joined the full-time staff after graduation.” Around that time, he received training in technical writing from an influential teacher, professor Joey Horobetz.
Bisset said he was later inspired to become a Christian while playing religious programming on a station. “Becoming a Christian gave me tremendous encouragement,” he would say later.
He was eventually promoted to WFAX chief engineer. That same year, he and fellow engineer Henry Stewart launched a contract engineering business.
He earned an AAS in Broadcast Engineering Technology cum laude from Northern Virginia

articles.title_orig: AEM Brings Industry Leaders Together at World Dairy Expo to Talk Association Involvement and Program Value - AEM | Association of Equipment Manufacturers
articles.title_zh: AEM Brings Industry Leaders Together at World Dairy Expo to Talk Association Involvement and Program Value - AEM | Association of Equipment Manufacturers
articles.content_orig:
The dairy equipment industry faces no shortage of challenges, from emerging technologies and regulatory hurdles to shifting customer demands and evolving market conditions. Addressing those challenges often requires more than individual company expertise – it requires collaboration from across the industry.
That spirit of collaboration was on full display as AEM's dairy-focused committees gathered during the 59th World Dairy Expo held last week in Madison, Wisconsin. The meetings brought together dairy equipment manufacturers and industry leaders to discuss market trends, committee priorities, and the value of continued engagement in AEM programs and initiatives. AEM hosted its Dairy Equipment Engineering Committee , the Dairy Equipment Leadership Group , and the Dairy Equipment Statistics Committee for meetings during the event.
A highlight of the gathering was a member panel featuring representatives from dairy and agriculture-focused AEM member companies, who shared firsthand perspectives on the benefits of participating in AEM committees and Market Share Statistics programs .
One recurring theme throughout the discussion was the power of industry data to support smarter decision-making.
Attendees noted that participation in AEM's Market Share Statistics programs provides members with access to timely industry intelligence, helping companies better understand market dynamics and evaluate business opportunities. In addition to strengthening individual business planning, the collective data helps create a more complete picture of industry trends.
One member shared how AEM helped demonstrate the value of market intelligence as emerging technologies began gaining traction in the dairy sector.
"When we were struggling to break into an emerging area, AEM used real-world examples from other equipment sectors to show the value of industry data," said GEA Farm Technologies’ Adam Burns. "If organizations are wondering how data can help them, AEM can show people the data and show them how other industries are using it, and they will start to see that value."
Panelists emphasized that access to reliable market data becomes even more impactful when paired with external economic indicators and market intelligence through AEM’s Business Intelligence, allowing companies to make more informed strategic decisions.
Beyond market intelligence, members highlighted the importance of AEM committees as a forum for industry problem-solving.
As new technologies and equipment categories emerge, manufacturers often encounter common challenges, including product classifications, standards questions, and regulatory considerations. Rather than tackling those issues independently, AEM committees create an environment where members can discuss concerns, share experiences, and work toward common solutions.
"When members have questions about new equipment or emerging technologies, we can come together as an industry and find solutions instead of struggling alone," said DeLaval’s Chris Horton. "Trying to solve those challenges collectively benefits everyone."
That collaborative approach helps reduce duplication of effort while supporting the long-term health of both the dairy equipment industry and the producers it serves.
As the dairy industry continues to evolve, collaboration remains one of its greatest strengths. By leveraging data, sharing experiences, and working toward common goals, AEM members are helping build a stronger, more resilient future for dairy equipment manufacturers and the producers they serve. The conversations held in Madison demonstrated that when the industry comes together, the result is more than valuable insight. It is a collective commitment to advancing the success of the dairy sector for years to come.
For more information on AEM’s agriculture services, contact AEM’s Austin Gellings at agellings@aem.org . For more information on AEM Market Share Statistics, contact AEM's Jacquelyn LaFavor at jlafavor@aem.org .

articles.title_orig: WashU rises to No. 16 in the U.S. News and World Report’s rankings
articles.title_zh: WashU rises to No. 16 in the U.S. News and World Report’s rankings
articles.content_orig:
WashU moved up from 20th place to 16th place in the 2026 U.S. News and World Report national rankings.
This is the highest WashU has ranked on the list since 2022, when it was in 14th place. In 2023, WashU dropped to 24th and since then has had a steady increase up the list to reach 16th this year, tied with Brown University, Rice University, and Vanderbilt University, which had each previously been ranked higher than WashU.
In a statement to Student Life, Provost Mark D. West wrote that the University was pleased to learn about WashU’s new ranking, but the ranking was not representative of WashU as a whole.
“I certainly understand and respect that prospective families, employers, faculty, alumni, and others pay close attention to rankings. They can be important. However, regardless of where we are ranked, rankings are a pale reflection of our strengths, and they don’t define our mission,” West wrote. “They cannot capture all that we, or any other institution, stand for. Our focus remains on advancing our mission and investing in the people and work that make WashU an exceptional university.”
Sophomore Wole Adeoye said that he thought WashU may have earned its new position in the rankings through its efforts to improve student experience through alumni engagement and professor relationships, which have helped to increase national recognition.
“I think it wasn’t surprising that we’re at that level of caliber of the schools we were tied with. However, I do think it’s surprising from a national perspective, since WashU wasn’t regarded as highly in the past,” Adeoye said. “Even a few years ago we were 24th, and so I think seeing that rapid growth is a surprise, but I think it’s well deserved.”
Junior Courtney Lucas II said he understands why rankings are relevant for high school applicants to understand a school’s prestige when they are applying, but they lose their significance once students get to college.
“I wish we valued rankings a little bit less, but I understand that, especially in this economy, people want to get a bang for their buck with tuition and things like that,” Lucas said. “So I also recognize why people focus on them, but I think we can kind of start to move away from rankings a little bit more, especially as we get older and more mature.”
Junior Cara Satyr explained that rankings, however, do hold some weight once students graduate and enter the job market as applicants may seem more appealing to an employer if they attended a highly ranked school.
“I think that in an employment world, employers like to find candidates who go to top schools and who have that on their resume,” Satyr said. “The ability to even say that you went to a high ranked school can differentiate you from other candidates. So I don’t think it’s fair to say they don’t matter at all.”
First-year Seoha Kim explained that rankings are just a small part of what made him choose to attend WashU, highlighting the importance of making sure that a school is a good match based on a variety of factors.
“If you like the vibe of the school, then I think that’s what matters more. For some people, if they go to a really prestigious school then they might struggle with making friends or dealing with academics,” Kim said. “ If the school doesn’t fit you, then I think there’s no point. So the rank doesn’t really matter because their own well-being and happiness matters more.”
Adeoye echoed Kim’s sentiment that while WashU’s ranking is a source of pride, its placement on the list does not matter as much as the environment of the school and has a minimal effect on the success of its students going forward.
“I think it’s something the students do see and they do appreciate it, and I think we take pride in our ranking,” Adeoye said. “But I don’t think that’s the only thing that defines us.”

articles.title_orig: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.title_zh: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.content_orig:
A webinar on 16 October will commemorate World Food Day and say farewell to the UN special rapporteur for the Right to Water and Sanitation.
The webinar will take the World Food Day theme “ Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” The discussion will explore what innovation can look like when we place food security, water, land, human rights, and ecological sustainability at the centre.
World Food Day is observed on 16 October each year and provides an opportunity to draw attention to hunger and food insecurity while strengthening collective action towards food systems that are sustainable, equitable, and resilient. This year ’ s webinar will bring together United Nations mandate holders, faith-based organisations, civil society organisations, and community practitioners to explore some of the challenges shaping food insecurity today – including poverty, unsustainable agricultural practices and climate change – and to share approaches that are contributing to resilience, food sovereignty, and sustainable livelihoods.
The session will also provide an opportunity to hear from Prof. Pedro Arrojo-Agudo, UN special rapporteur on the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation, whose six-year mandate concludes in November 2026.

articles.title_orig: Highest Mortgage Rates in 3 Years Chills the Housing Market
articles.title_zh: Highest Mortgage Rates in 3 Years Chills the Housing Market
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

articles.title_orig: Old World, Al Fresco At the English Inn
articles.title_zh: Old World, Al Fresco At the English Inn
articles.content_orig:
Randy Daubner created a problem at The English Inn, the Fish Creek restaurant he has owned for 21 years.
Shortly after he took over, he and his then-wife Lisa began building a patio near the entrance to give diners waiting for a table a place to have a drink outside. Pretty soon, those diners were willing to wait to eat outside, even when tables were available inside what had long been an upscale supper club dining room.
“It got so busy, I just kept building,”  Daubner said. “We added more tables, more plantings, more fires and lighting.”
During a spring visit to the restaurant, a landscaper was finding places for dozens more bushes and trees for the patio, which now has space for 150 diners.
The multi-level patio vibe is both light and cozy, with nooks for tables nestled around a fountain and koi pond built by WaterScape Designs. It’s lined with hundreds of flowers, trees and bushes. Diners still enjoy the restaurant’s old fashioneds, Manhattans and classic dishes like Beef Wellington and prime rib, but now in the glow of the 40 fires that light and warm tables and draw attention to a restaurant that could otherwise be overlooked.
Before the outdoor expansion,“the parking lot was large and tired, there was no lighting, and people thought the place was closed,” Daubner said.
A massive metal sculpture of a dragonfly on one end of the parking lot and a knight on horseback on the other side now assures that the restaurant can’t be missed.
It’s a much different face from the inside of this longtime county landmark. Once home to The Parkway restaurant, it became The English Inn when Pete and Dort Kortes bought it in 1964. A drawbridge guides diners over the koi pond at the front door, where they open the wooden doors to the dim lowlight of the bar and lounge, a throwback to another era. The ceiling sits low above the bar that seems to hug you as you enter and prepares you for a dining room unlike any other around.
Around the bar you find a hulking stone fireplace on the north wall and custom-crafted metal chandeliers overhead; stained-glass partitions and dining nooks are framed by bulky wooden beams. It all comes together to create a vibe that’s part English pub and part Knights of the Round Table just a little north of Fish Creek on state Highway 42.
“This was all Dort’s vision,” Daubner said. “These are still her original wooden chairs. They don’t make them like this anymore.”
It’s a dining room made for the cool nights of winter, and a patio perfect for the warm nights of summer.
The English Inn is located at 3713 Hwy 42 in Fish Creek.

articles.title_orig: Second measles case confirmed in Allegheny County
articles.title_zh: Second measles case confirmed in Allegheny County
articles.content_orig:
Check out our $15 ish Pittsburgh Meal Map
A child who attends a private Christian school in the North Hills has been infected with measles, the second confirmed case in Allegheny County.
Pennsylvania is facing the largest outbreak of measles in the country, with more than 1,000 cases and five deaths across the commonwealth. The first case of measles for an Allegheny County resident was identified last week, with possible exposures at a Target on McKnight Road in McCandless. The Allegheny County Health Department reported previously that case of measles did not include a school exposure .
A spokesperson for the department confirmed there has been a second reported case of measles and that the agency is working with officials at the student’s school to contain the spread. The department declined to  provide details about the second person who is infected, citing privacy.
A spokesperson for Eden Christian Academy, which operates three North Hills campuses, acknowledged its student body was impacted. Eden Christian enrolls 658 students across  elementary schools in Ross and Pine, and a school for upper grades in Ohio Township. The spokesperson did not say which campus was impacted.
Health Department spokesperson Ronnie Das said staff have “been providing specific guidance to the school nurse and administration of an impacted school on how to organize lists of immune staff and students and ensuring school staff understands who needs to quarantine and for how long.”
Eden Christian Academy released a statement to Public Source about the school’s response on Thursday, saying the school could not release any identifying information due to privacy laws. “We are working directly with the Health Department to implement their protocol,” the official said. “Families and staff have received notification with instructions from public health authorities.”
The school’s vaccination rate is 81%, which is in the bottom 10% of schools in Allegheny County. It’s lower than the 92-95% threshold required for herd immunity, and below the Health Department’s target of at least 95%. The school didn’t respond to a question about whether it is doing anything to try to increase its vaccination rates.
“The health, safety, and well-being of our students, faculty, staff, and families is our highest priority,” the school said in its statement.
In June, Public Source reported that private religious schools generally have the lowest measles vaccination rates in the county , with children in the youngest grades showing the lowest rates. At the time health experts in the county said they did not know of any specific efforts to try to improve vaccination rates at parochial schools.
“We are very concerned about the fact that there are these pockets” of students who are at risk, Allegheny County’s Medical Director Jillian Irwin said in May.
The Health Department said in a statement today that it works with school officials to review attendance records and see which students might have been exposed because infected individuals can spread the disease for four days before and after symptoms appear. The department recommends quarantines for students and family members who have been exposed to measles and have not been vaccinated or previously infected. The department recommends isolation for students with confirmed cases.
“Anyone with measles needs to isolate from others during this time,” Das said. “Nonimmune household members must quarantine. Immune household members do not have to quarantine.”
Lisa Bruce was attending a conference about special needs children at a church that is physically connected to — though unaffiliated with — the Eden Christian Academy building in Pine on Thursday. She has an 18-year-old in college about an hour from Pittsburgh, she said, so she isn’t worried for her daughter. But she has two elderly parents in their 80s and doesn’t know if their old vaccinations will be as effective at their age. ( The CDC’s website says people born before 1957 are presumed to be immune.)
“It worries me that people are not being vaccinated,” Bruce said. “Being vaccinated is a choice.”
Correction: The original version of this story indicated an incorrect number of statewide measles cases.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela's Maduro charged in US with ordering torture of opponents, Americans
articles.title_zh: Venezuela's Maduro charged in US with ordering torture of opponents, Americans
articles.content_orig:
Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro has been charged by U.S. authorities with torture and other crimes in a new indictment unsealed Thursday that adds pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking offenses.
Maduro, who was previously charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., is now also facing allegations of human rights abuses during his reign as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.
Both have pleaded not guilty in the criminal case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They had already been facing potential life prison sentences if convicted.
Cilia Flores was scheduled to be in court Thursday, where her lawyers will urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she has “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital when care was needed.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence.”

articles.title_orig: Video: China Coast Guard Uses Water Cannon During Philippine Medevac
articles.title_zh: Video: China Coast Guard Uses Water Cannon During Philippine Medevac
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-08 14:50:00
The Philippine Coast Guard has reported another dust-up at Second Thomas Shoal, where the Philippine Navy maintains an outpost aboard a deteriorating shipwreck in order to deter Chinese expansion within Manila's exclusive economic zone.
Second Thomas Shoal has been an on-again, off-again flashpoint for tensions between Philippine and Chinese forces in the Spratly Islands since at least 1999, when the Philippine Navy intentionally grounded the WWII-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre on the reef to serve as a base. The service has maintained a small detachment of marines on board the wreck ever since, and the periodic resupply and rotation missions to and from the shoal are a recurring source of friction. In times of heightened diplomatic tension, the China Coast Guard has often attempted to prevent PCG personnel from reaching the station, periodically adopting forcible methods like aggressive maneuvering and water-cannoning.
The latest encounter occurred on October 8, according to PCG spokesman Jay Tarriela. A Navy servicemember aboard BRP Sierra Madre was in need of medical attention and required evacuation from the station, and the PCG was tasked with mounting a medevac mission. On Thursday morning, the patrol vessel BRP Cabra departed Lawak and got under way for Second Thomas Shoal. At about 0730 hours, Cabra arrived at a position about nine nautical miles away from the reef, where it encountered a familiar presence: China Coast Guard cutter CCG 5306. The CCG crew turned on their water cannon and closed the distance to Cabra, approaching to within 400 yards, Cabra's crew reported. The Chinese cutter's maneuvering prevented further progress towards the Philippine base.
In order to avoid getting hit by the water cannon, BRP Cabra stayed about 13 miles offshore and waited. The crew had hoped to conduct a rendezvous and transfer closer to the patient, but this was not possible because of the Chinese presence, Tarriela said.
By early afternoon, the situation had not changed. To adapt, Cabra's crew launched a team in its RIB boat, and the BRP Sierra Madre station dispatched two inflatable rubber boats with the patient and escort personnel. They met up about four nautical miles off the reef and transferred the patient between boats. Throughout the evolution, CCG small boats and cutters harassed the PCG boat crews, Tarriela said, using "dangerous" maneuvers. Other Chinese vessels involved or in the area included CCG cutters 5009 and 21585, plus the PLA Navy frigate Yongzhou (628) and one maritime militia fishing vessel.
After bringing the patient safely aboard, the Cabra's crew provided him with a checkup and with IV fluids, then got under way to deliver him to shore for a higher level of care.
According to the PCG, the CCG's interference delayed the medevac for hours and created danger for Philippine personnel and the patient. In a statement, Tarriela also highlighted the root of the longstanding sovereignty dispute: China claims a right to control navigation within the western Philippine EEZ, despite a 2016 international arbitral ruling to the contrary.
"When a life is at stake, there should be no water cannon, no obstruction, and no delay. Saving a sick or injured person at sea is a basic obligation that every coast guard in the world is expected to uphold. We call on the CCG to value and respect humanitarian missions moving forward, and to act in a manner consistent with international law and the professional standards expected of any coast guard," PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan said in a statement.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
As in prior incidents, the China Coast Guard claimed that it had permitted PCG units to access Chinese territory within the Philippine EEZ.
"China on Thursday allowed the Philippine Coast Guard vessel 4409 to evacuate an injured person from a Philippine vessel illegally grounded at [Second Thomas Shoal], permitting a small-boat transfer on humanitarian grounds, and the China Coast Guard (CCG) handled the operation in accordance with the law and provided necessary assistance," CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue told state-owned Chinese outlet Global Times.

articles.title_orig: 2 Latvians Arrested after Breaching Perimeter of RAF Molesworth, UK Air Base Used by US
articles.title_zh: 2 Latvians Arrested after Breaching Perimeter of RAF Molesworth, UK Air Base Used by US
articles.content_orig:
British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday.
The arrests come weeks after a suspected plot targeting another British airbase used by the US military raised concerns about security at military sites across Britain.
Police said there was nothing so far to suggest the incident at RAF Molesworth in eastern England was linked to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by the US military to launch missions against Iran.
The men were discovered after Ministry of Defence Police found an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol at RAF Molesworth, about 100 km (60 miles) north of London, and raised the alarm.
Subsequent checks uncovered a small breach in the perimeter fence and the two men, aged 32 and 36, were arrested inside the base.
They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage, before being re-arrested on suspicion of “entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK” under the National Security Act 2023.
RAF Molesworth is used by US personnel and hosts intelligence analysis and command operations, as well as a NATO intelligence centre. It is not used for flying operations.
Last month, several men were arrested over a suspected plot to attack RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) ‌west of London. The British government has linked the suspected plot to Iran , which denied any involvement.
The incident raised concerns over security at Britain’s military bases, particularly those used by US forces. The US said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of its bombers from Fairford.
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement.
Police said both men were resident in Britain and that officers were searching two addresses in the area around Peterborough, a nearby city.
Bomb disposal officers checked the abandoned vehicle but found nothing of concern, police said.
“We are highly vigilant about potential threats to our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” defense minister Wes Streeting said in a post on X.
A US Air Force spokesperson said they appreciated the swift response and support from local law enforcement.
“We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities,” the spokesperson added.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices face new threat as Hurricane Isaias forces widespread Gulf oil shutdowns
articles.title_zh: Gas prices face new threat as Hurricane Isaias forces widespread Gulf oil shutdowns
articles.content_orig:
A powerful storm snaking its way through the Gulf of Mexico threatens to disrupt U.S. oil and gasoline production at a moment when retail gas and diesel prices are squeezing American consumers and companies.
Hurricane Isaias is rapidly intensifying and expected to make landfall along the northeastern Gulf shore late Friday or early Saturday.
Already, major oil companies, including Chevron and Shell, have begun shutting down some oil production sites. Chevron said it was shutting down four of its assets in the Gulf, although production at its five other facilities in the region remained at normal levels. Shell said it was halting production at five sites.
All told, nearly two-thirds of Gulf oil production and 57% of natural gas production had been shut in by noon Thursday, according to the U.S. Marine Minerals Administration.
Hurricanes and major storms are common in the region, so oil companies have well-established evacuation and shutdown protocols.
Still, the timing could hardly be worse for U.S. consumers.
The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has spawned broader regional conflict, which continues to disrupt energy supplies and drive oil and gasoline prices higher.
Global benchmark Brent crude oil prices surged nearly 5% in early Thursday trading amid reports that President Donald Trump was considering renewed attacks against Iran. U.S. gasoline prices averaged $4.36, down slightly from a week ago but still up 21 cents over the past month.
“This could not have come at a worse time as gasoline and diesel inventories are quite low,” Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates LLC consultancy, wrote in a note Wednesday.
Nearly all U.S. offshore production is in Isaias’ path, he wrote, which means “the impact, even short-lived, can be significant.”
Lipow estimated that 14% of the nation’s refining capacity is in the storm’s path. Given that most U.S. refineries are now running at maximum levels in response to the global squeeze on capacity, “There is no slack in the system,” he wrote.
Oil is a globally traded commodity, so any reduction in supplies will send prices higher around the world.
Refineries in the path of Isaias are likely to see flooding that could take them offline for up to 10 days, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. That is expected to produce a short-term squeeze for U.S. gasoline prices.
But for U.S. motorists, the bigger concerns remain overseas — especially in Russia, where Ukraine continues to target refineries.
“The refining problem is looking like, short to medium term, at least three to six months,” De Haan said. “And it sounds like it’s going to be continuing, especially with Ukraine promising to target more Russian refineries. So there needs to be some de-escalation there for there to be any relief, but it doesn’t look like we’re seeing it.”
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
